ui.hero.lead: Almost every antipsychotic acts at the dopamine D2 receptor, a class A G-protein-coupled receptor that signals through Gαi/o. First-generation agents are competitive antagonists; most second-generation agents combine D2 antagonism with 5-HT2A blockade; and the newest class are D2 partial agonists that occupy the receptor while leaving part of its signaling intact. Because antagonism is competitive, occupancy depends on the local dopamine concentration, which differs between the dopaminergic pathways - the reason one plasma concentration produces a therapeutic effect in one pathway and adverse effects in another. This resource integrates receptor structure, binding profiles, drug properties and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models.
ui.hero.title: Antipsychotics & the D<sub>2</sub> receptor

ui.notes.calibration: Dose-occupancy calibration. Each drug carries one parameter (the plasma concentration of the D2-active moiety giving 50 % striatal D2 occupancy) fitted to published PET studies, mostly with 11C-raclopride, so that the model reproduces the reported occupancy at the studied doses (for example clozapine 75-900 mg/day: 16-69 % in the model, 16-68 % reported). It conflates plasma and brain concentrations and ignores active transport at the blood-brain barrier - which is why amisulpride, risperidone and paliperidone raise prolactin more than their striatal occupancy would suggest: the pituitary lies outside the barrier. Different radioligands give different values; for lurasidone, a 18F-fallypride study in patients suggests markedly lower occupancy than the 11C-raclopride study used here.
ui.notes.clinicalScope: Clinical scope. Dose equivalents, monitoring recommendations and the summarized indications are teaching simplifications; they differ between national formularies and guidelines and are not a substitute for a current label or guideline.
ui.notes.occupancyModel: Occupancy model. Occupancy follows mass-action binding at equilibrium. Dopamine is treated as a single competing concentration per pathway, with one effective KDA; in reality receptors exist in high- and low-affinity states, dopamine fluctuates phasically on a millisecond-to-second scale, and agonist affinity depends on G-protein coupling. Receptor reserve, internalization and up-regulation during chronic treatment (relevant to dopamine supersensitivity and tardive dyskinesia) are not represented.
ui.notes.parameterValues: Parameter values. Receptor affinities (Ki) are taken from section 12.2 of the FDA label where it states them, and otherwise are the ChEMBL median for human receptors, compared with the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology; reported values for the same drug and receptor often differ between laboratories by 3-10-fold. Half-lives, volumes of distribution, protein binding and bioavailability come from the FDA labels (section 12.3) where available. The source of each value, the value reported there and its status (consistent, calibrated, model assumption or not yet verified) are listed in the searchable data tables; the older generic labels of haloperidol, chlorpromazine and fluphenazine contain no pharmacokinetic data, so those values are not yet sourced.
ui.notes.partialAgonism: Partial agonism. Intrinsic activity is modeled as a single number per drug and receptor, applied to one signaling output. In reality it is pathway-dependent (G-protein versus β-arrestin, functional selectivity) and varies with receptor density and the tissue measured, so the values here describe a tendency rather than a fixed quantity.
ui.notes.pharmacokineticModel: Pharmacokinetic model. One compartment with first-order absorption and elimination; distribution phases are therefore absent. Absorption rate constants were fitted to the time to peak in the FDA labels; as an independent check, the model predicts a steady-state peak of ≈ 306 ng/mL for clozapine 100 mg twice daily, against 319 ng/mL in the label. Depot products are modeled with release phases fitted to the labels and summaries of product characteristics: a fraction released at once or after a lag, or at a constant rate over a release window, each through a first-order absorption step. This reproduces delayed release (Risperdal Consta from week 3), double peaks (Perseris, Uzedy, Okedi) and the time to peak of palmitate depots, but not the variation between injection sites or patients. Initiation regimens of the labels (loading injections, Aristada Initio, 1-day starts and oral overlap) are simulated separately and added, as the model is linear. Regional half-lives (EU summaries of product characteristics) change the shape of the curve but not the exposure: clearance stays at the calibrated base value, so plasma EC50 values apply in every region. Concentrations of the parent drug and its D2-active metabolites are summed without adjustment for differing affinity, and only metabolites flagged as D2-active enter the sum.
ui.notes.regionalDistribution: Regional distribution. Abundance levels are a qualitative summary of receptor autoradiography, in situ hybridization and PET, partly in rodent brain. Levels are relative within each receptor and not comparable in absolute density between receptors. Each structure is shaded uniformly, so laminar and nuclear differences (for example 5-HT2A concentrated in cortical layer V, or D3 in the nucleus accumbens shell) appear only in the descriptions. The choroid plexus, which carries the highest 5-HT2C density, is not part of the brain model.
ui.notes.structure: Receptor structure. The displayed structure is a thermostabilized crystal construct with a fused lysozyme in place of intracellular loop 3 (removed here) and several stabilizing mutations; the extracellular loops and the amino terminus are partly unresolved. Drugs other than risperidone, haloperidol and dopamine are shown on the risperidone pose, so their binding geometry is not modeled. The inactive-to-active morph interpolates linearly between two experimental structures and is not a simulation of the activation pathway; the lipid bilayer is drawn schematically.
ui.notes.thresholds: Occupancy thresholds. The 65 %, 72 % and 78 % thresholds for antipsychotic response, prolactin elevation and extrapyramidal symptoms are group-level findings from small PET studies of mainly first-generation agents (Kapur et al. 2000; Farde et al. 1992) and vary between individuals. Clozapine and quetiapine are effective at considerably lower striatal occupancy, which the thresholds do not explain; rapid dissociation from D2 (Kapur & Seeman 2001) and contributions from other receptors have been proposed as reasons.

ui.pd.crAntagonist: Competitive antagonism. {drug} shifts the dopamine concentration-response curve to the right in parallel, without lowering its maximum: enough dopamine always displaces the drug. Occupancy therefore depends on both the drug concentration and the local dopamine concentration, which is why the same plasma level produces different occupancy in different pathways. At present: {signal} signaling versus {base} without drug.
ui.pd.crNoD2: No D2 binding. {drug} does not bind D2: the dopamine concentration-response curve is unchanged at any concentration, so the drug curves coincide with dopamine alone.
ui.pd.crNoDrug: Competition with dopamine. Select a drug to see how it shifts the dopamine concentration-response curve.
ui.pd.crPartial: Partial agonism. {drug} has intrinsic activity {ia} at D2, so bound receptors keep signaling at {iaPct} % of the dopamine-bound level. The curve is therefore both shifted right and clamped: it cannot fall below the drug's own level (a floor) and cannot rise to the dopamine maximum (a ceiling). Where dopamine is low the drug raises signaling above the untreated level, and where dopamine is high it lowers it - the basis of the term "dopamine stabilizer". At present: {signal} signaling versus {base} without drug.
ui.pd.doseIntro: Dose and occupancy. Steady-state striatal D2 occupancy as a function of daily dose, computed from the pharmacokinetic model and calibrated so that each drug reproduces its published PET occupancy. Occupancy saturates, so above the usual range large dose increases buy little extra occupancy while exposure, and with it the adverse-effect burden, keeps rising in proportion.
ui.pd.doseNoD2: Dose and occupancy. {drug} does not bind D2, so the PET window of striatal D2 occupancy does not apply; plasma levels by dose are shown under Pharmacokinetics.
ui.pd.doseNotReached: {lo} % is not reached within the plotted range.
ui.pd.doseNote: Occupancy thresholds ({a} %, {b} %, {c} %) are those reported by Kapur et al. 2000 from <sup>11</sup>C-raclopride PET, which measures the striatum at tonic dopamine levels.
ui.pd.dosePartial: As a partial agonist (intrinsic activity {ia} at D<sub>2</sub>), {drug} reaches high occupancy at usual doses while leaving ≈ {iaPct} % of signaling intact, so occupancy and functional blockade are not the same quantity here and the occupancy thresholds do not transfer directly.
ui.pd.dosePathways: The curves separate by pathway because the same drug concentration competes against different local dopamine concentrations: at the raised mesolimbic level used here ({da} nM) the same dose gives ≈ {occ}.
ui.pd.doseUsual: For {drug}, {dose} mg/day gives ≈ {occ} at tonic striatal dopamine ({da} nM);
ui.pd.funcLayer: Agonism: −log₁₀ EC₅₀ at the receptor (M, lab)
ui.pd.funcSummary: The stars mark where the drug activates the receptor, at the EC<sub>50</sub> measured in cell assays (ChEMBL medians): {list}. Laboratory E<sub>max</sub> depends on receptor expression and is usually higher than the intrinsic activity in the brain.
ui.pd.intro: Competitive binding at D2 between drug (concentration C, dissociation constant Ki) and dopamine ([DA], KDA): the fractional occupancy is θ = (C/Ki) / (1 + C/Ki + [DA]/KDA), and receptor signaling is E = ([DA]/KDA + α·C/Ki) / (1 + C/Ki + [DA]/KDA), where α is the intrinsic activity of the drug (α = 0 for an antagonist, 0 < α < 1 for a partial agonist). The functional blockade that drives clinical effect is therefore θ·(1 − α), which is why a partial agonist can occupy most receptors without abolishing signaling.
ui.pd.logScale: Scale: log₁₀, each ring a tenfold step (innermost {inner}, outermost {outer})
ui.pd.occNoDrug: Receptor occupancy. Select a drug to display its concentration-occupancy relationship at each target.
ui.pd.occSummary: Receptor occupancy. Fractional occupancy θ = C / (C + Ki), so half-maximal occupancy occurs at Ki; at D2 the curve is shifted right by competition with synaptic dopamine, θD2 = (C/Ki) / (1 + C/Ki + [DA]/KDA). At {conc} with {da} nM dopamine: {list}. The order of the curves is the receptor profile that distinguishes the drugs of this class: targets lying to the left of D2 are occupied before an antipsychotic effect is reached, and their blockade accounts for much of the adverse-effect burden.
ui.pd.potencySummary: The dotted layer is the potency at each receptor: pEC<sub>50</sub>, from the plasma concentration that gives 50 % occupancy (EC<sub>50</sub>, {unit}: {ec50}). The dashed black ring is the steady-state plasma concentration at the usual dose ({dose} mg/day, {conc}); receptors whose potency point lies outside the ring are more than half occupied: {list}.
ui.pd.ratioD2: The 5-HT2A/D2 affinity ratio is {r}:1 in favor of D2 (the Meltzer index, > 1 for most second-generation agents).
ui.pd.ratioHt2a: The 5-HT2A/D2 affinity ratio is {r}:1 in favor of 5-HT2A (the Meltzer index, > 1 for most second-generation agents).
ui.pd.scale.title: Distance from the center (Kᵢ or EC₅₀):
ui.pd.selLayers: The solid layer is {drug}; the dashed layer is the co-formulated {list}.
ui.pd.selNoDrug: Receptor affinity profile. Select a drug to display its affinity at each target.
ui.pd.selNoKi: {drug}: no Kᵢ at the human receptors was found in the sources used; occupancy at D<sub>2</sub> comes from the PET-calibrated plasma EC<sub>50</sub>.
ui.pd.selNotDetermined: Kᵢ not determined (no human value found): {list}.
ui.pd.selSummary: Affinity profile. Radial distance is pKi = −log10Ki (Ki in M); one unit is a tenfold difference (pKi 9 ≈ 1 nM, 7 ≈ 100 nM). {drug} binds most tightly to {top} (Ki {topKi} nM); the order is {order}. {ratio} Targets plotted at the detection limit are not bound at clinically relevant concentrations.
ui.pd.title: Pharmacodynamics
ui.pk.accumDepot: Depot kinetics. Absorption from the injection site (t½ ≈ {tabs} days) is slower than elimination, so the apparent half-life is set by absorption (flip-flop kinetics): steady state takes months, and concentrations fall equally slowly after the last injection.
ui.pk.accumDepotIntro: Depot injections every {interval} ({product}). Each injection keeps releasing drug while the next is given, so pre-injection (trough) concentrations (◆) rise until release and elimination balance. In the model, the average level reaches 90 % of steady state {when}.
ui.pk.accumIntro: Accumulation at a dosing interval of {interval}. Each dose is given before the preceding one has been eliminated, so pre-dose (trough) concentrations (◆) rise until steady state. The accumulation ratio R = 1/(1 − e−kτ) relates steady-state to first-dose exposure.
ui.pk.accumItem: {name}: t½ ≈ {t12} → R ≈ {r}×, 90 % of steady state after ≈ {t90}
ui.pk.accumMetabolite: Active metabolite. {metabolite} (t½ ≈ {t12}) continues to accumulate after {drug} itself has reached steady state, so changes in dose take correspondingly longer to show their full effect.
ui.pk.accumSingle: Accumulation. During repeated dosing, concentrations rise until the rate of elimination equals the dosing rate; steady state is approached after 4-5 half-lives of the slowest species. For {drug} the slowest step has t½ ≈ {t12}, giving ≈ {tss} to steady state. Select Show accumulation to simulate repeated dosing.
ui.pk.accumSingleDepot: Accumulation. With injections every {interval}, concentrations rise until release from the depot and elimination balance. For {product}, the model reaches 90 % of the steady-state average {when}; release from the injection site, not elimination, sets this time. Select Show accumulation to simulate repeated injections.
ui.pk.accumTip: Repeat the dose until steady state is reached
ui.pk.cmpAxisX: Time after a single oral dose (days)
ui.pk.cmpSummary: Duration of exposure. Concentration of the D2-active moiety after a single oral dose, normalized to each drug's own peak, so that only the time course is compared. Time from peak to 50 % of Cmax: {list}{mods}. Half-lives of this class span two orders of magnitude, which determines how long dose changes take to take full effect and how quickly concentrations fall if doses are missed: quetiapine is cleared within a day, whereas the active metabolites of aripiprazole and cariprazine persist for weeks.
ui.pk.componentNote: {name} ({dose} mg per dose, from the capsule strength) is simulated with its own kinetics: t½ ≈ {t12}; clearance pathways {pathways}.
ui.pk.initTip: Initiation regimen of the product label: loading injections or oral overlap before and with the first maintenance injections
ui.pk.intro: One-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination, including chains of active metabolites (9-hydroxyrisperidone after risperidone, dehydroaripiprazole after aripiprazole, the two sequential metabolites of cariprazine) and patient- and interaction-related modifiers acting on specific elimination pathways (CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP3A4, glucuronidation, renal excretion). Depot injections are absorption-limited, so their apparent half-life is set by release from the injection site rather than by elimination.
ui.pk.metabolismIntro: Most antipsychotics undergo hepatic oxidation by CYP1A2, CYP2D6 or CYP3A4, several by direct glucuronidation, and two (paliperidone, amisulpride) are largely excreted unchanged by the kidney. Active metabolites with half-lives longer than the parent drug determine how long dose changes take to take full effect. These pathways determine the modifier effects simulated above.

ui.safety.boxedDementia: Increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Analyses of placebo-controlled trials of atypical antipsychotics in this population showed a risk of death in drug-treated patients of between 1.6 and 1.7 times that in placebo-treated patients; conventional antipsychotics carry a comparable or greater risk. No antipsychotic is approved for the treatment of dementia-related psychosis except brexpiprazole for agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia, and pimavanserin for hallucinations and delusions of Parkinson disease psychosis.
ui.safety.boxedSuicidality: Antidepressant-class warnings additionally apply to the agents licensed as adjuncts in major depressive disorder (aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, quetiapine XR, olanzapine-fluoxetine), which carry the boxed warning on suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents and young adults.
ui.safety.cardiac: Cardiac. ECG before and during treatment where QTc prolongation is a concern (high-dose or intravenous haloperidol, ziprasidone, pimozide, amisulpride, or co-prescribed QT-prolonging drugs), and with risk factors or electrolyte disturbance.
ui.safety.clozapine: Clozapine-specific. Absolute neutrophil count on a mandatory schedule; troponin and C-reactive protein if myocarditis is suspected in the first 8 weeks; active enquiry about constipation; plasma levels when efficacy, adherence, smoking change or infection is in question.
ui.safety.intro: The adverse-effect burden of this class follows directly from the receptor profiles in Receptor targets and the exposure in Pharmacokinetics. Baseline and periodic monitoring is recommended for all agents, with drug-specific additions.
ui.safety.metabolic: Metabolic. Weight and waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and a lipid profile at baseline, at 3 months, then at least annually; more often with clozapine, olanzapine and quetiapine, and in children and adolescents, in whom weight gain is greater.
ui.safety.movement: Movement disorders. Examination for parkinsonism, akathisia, acute dystonia and tardive dyskinesia at baseline and at each review (for example with the AIMS or a comparable scale), particularly with first-generation agents and stronger D2 blockade.
ui.safety.nms: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome. A rare, potentially fatal reaction (fever, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability, raised creatine kinase) requiring immediate withdrawal of the drug and supportive treatment.
ui.safety.prolactin: Prolactin. Measure when symptoms suggest elevation (menstrual disturbance, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia); highest with amisulpride, risperidone, paliperidone and first-generation agents.
ui.safety.title: Safety & monitoring

ui.st.partialAgonistText: Occupies {occ} % of receptors and signals at {ia} % of the dopamine-bound level, so the conformational equilibrium lies between the two states.

ui.subst.cls.fgaDesc: D2 antagonist ("typical"); extrapyramidal symptoms and prolactin elevation are dose-limiting
ui.subst.cls.nonD2Desc: acts without D2 blockade (5-HT2A inverse agonist or muscarinic agonist)
ui.subst.cls.paDesc: third-generation; intrinsic activity 0.15-0.3 at D2, so high occupancy without full blockade
ui.subst.cls.sgaDesc: 5-HT2A antagonism alongside D2 ("atypical"); metabolic effects more prominent
ui.subst.footer: Selecting a row applies the substance to the mechanism, pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic simulations. Equivalent oral doses correspond to olanzapine 10 mg/day: half of the doses judged clinically equivalent to olanzapine 20 mg/day in the Second International Consensus Study of Antipsychotic Dosing (ICSAD-2, McAdam et al. 2023). Long-acting injectables are given as each product's standard dose for that oral dose (label or summary of product characteristics). Half-lives of long-acting injectables are apparent (absorption-limited) half-lives.

ui.substances.title: Antipsychotic substances
ui.targets.distIntro: Relative abundance of each receptor by brain region on a brain model built from neuroimaging templates, shown as a rotatable 3D model or as a 2D map rendered from it; one hemisphere is translucent to expose the deep structures (thalamus, striatum, hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus), brainstem and cerebellum. Select a receptor to switch the map. The four dopaminergic pathways are drawn on the model as colored tracts, with pulses running from the origin nucleus to the targets. Hover over a structure or a pathway for details.
ui.targets.distTitle: Regional distribution of the target receptors and dopaminergic pathways
ui.targets.intro: Antipsychotics are not selective: each binds a characteristic set of aminergic receptors, and the order of its affinities determines which effects appear at therapeutic doses. Blockade of D2 underlies the antipsychotic effect, extrapyramidal symptoms and prolactin elevation; blockade of 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, H1, M1 and α1 accounts for much of the remaining clinical profile. The cards below show each target with its live occupancy for the drug and concentration selected in Competitive antagonism at the receptor (kept in sync with Pharmacodynamics); selecting a card shows that receptor in the distribution map.
ui.targets.title: Receptor targets & clinical effects
